The show must go on

Nov 14, 2026 · 9 MIN READ · · BRANDON T. BANDE

  • zimbabwe
  • personal-branding
  • leadership
  • tech-community

Hi,

I'm Brandon.

Everyone wants to have their mascot wave and welcome 24/7 non-stop, we all want the clown to perform endlessly and the singer to hold the note forever. Business or entertainment, it doesn't matter - the cogs in the machine must play their part. The script must be followed and the show must go on. However, there comes a time when the people behind call it a day and pack their bags. Whether it is for passion or for profit, there comes a time when it is all draining.

For me, the final moment was at 2.00am, on an airport taxi. Half asleep after a tiring day organising an event and doing my last round of airport drop-offs. My body had taken can after can of caffeine and sugar through energy drinks and soft drinks. Around that time, I had taken one earlier but this time, it hadn't worked. Like my motivation, my body could take no more and it eventually caved in. I dozed off on the front seat. All the way to my hotel. And when I woke up about four hours later, I knew I was done. It was the time for me to go. I knew it, and it had to be done.

The beginning of the end

I entered 2026, all in. Ready to go all in to serve the communities that I served. Then bit by bit, I dropped out of things. For different reasons, but the constant factor in all was I no longer believed in what I was into. In one of my engagements, I had a cockamamie seat. Constantly talked over and brushed aside. Ego aside, if things worked out well - I would grumpily step aside. But in 2026, it has been disaster after disaster. And what has bothered me the most has been the fact that most of it was avoidable. I saw it, I called it and unfortunately no one batted an eye until it was time for me to chip in and try to save the day (I am no Batman, at times I failed).

First were the differences in direction

Let's be honest, in the tech space I have positioned myself as a community builder. I have brought people together, organised, volunteered and even paid for event expenses. To me this has been a sacred role, that I so much believe in (one of my weaknesses - it's all business, Bee). For me, the impact was in the lives we touched, the opportunities we created for others, the people we inspired to be leaders and the connections we made. It was people. Connections. Tech. In that order. So when I realised that one of the organisations I was doing it for, was mainly focused on doing this for PR - it didn't sit well with me. Considering that in close to four years of representing them, organising events and facilitating partnerships, I had never gained event support (In some cases, I lost my money trying to cover the gap that I created in a collaboration they ended writing off because they were not the main partner.) What I lamented was not the money, but the fact that where I set out on helping people, I was supposed to be on a mission to collect bodies for attracting donor sponsorship. And the community I was hell-bent on building was nothing more than a dot on their impact map.

.... then came the game

You can never outhustle bad governance. I have heard that so many times and being a daredevil, I have tried to. If we were to be honest, the tech community in Zimbabwe is not as mature as it could be. In the entirety of my time leading some of the communities, I have tried to outwit the system, walking on eggshells, balancing egos and maneuvering moves that pointed towards certain outcomes. The price that I paid with? My mental health. In a space where inflated egos run supreme, has-beens still believing that they have relevance and gatekeeping and sabotage are dished once you step into someone's territory (with a white flag btw), I find myself no longer willing to play. Everyone believes that they are doing great and where I looked at everyone and saw a table where everyone could eat - others were in a duel to death for scraps that we were fed. The community is not that big, our skills are not that advanced and the environment is not that friendly. There I said it. One question? When was the last time you heard of a tech event that is not government/corporate affiliated, has good speakers and demonstrations and is open to the crowd? DevFest? Yes and no.

... leaving even when I have a budget

So the cat is now out of the bag. I am leaving GDG Harare. Having been there since 2022. Over the years we have hosted so many events, invited so many speakers and done so much. However, with growth some things start losing their meaning. For years I chased numbers. Because I thought numbers could get us buzz, then momentum, the sponsorship and the real impact. The beauty about it is that the bills were paid for, but the mental toll has become something that I can no longer bear. As I grow, I want growth. Not only in numbers, but also in quality. And that is where everything falls off. My demands have become too much. And the system was never designed to take that sudden change in direction at such scale. (BTW, quality not only in terms of technical skills but in being a community that people are actually proud of).

.... and choosing to watch from the stands

Remember scale? With over 2k people subscribed to GDG Harare, it's exciting to know that over the years, we have become a must-join community in the tech space. Every student, every junior at one time passes through us and looks forward to mentorship, networks and learning opportunities. And I feel like we let em down. Every time, and every year. Having been the face of that failure for years (since I was the POC for newbies in most cases), I firmly believe it's time for someone more technical to come and build from the foundation we created. And I would gladly let that happen now, than to drag a fast growing community to the pits (someone's words not mine). So I leave the show, before it peaks (so that it actually peaks).

... and I choose me

Being a community builder, especially in a space where you do not have guaranteed sponsors is hard. In between the events there is a lot of planning, unfruitful attempts to host events or gain support. You are forced to show up, even where and when you can't for the sake of maintaining relationships. Then one day, the only thing you think of when you wake up is strategy. Community. And now you find yourself a pseudo-father of hundreds of kids who look up to you for direction. At the same time, you are a slave to the last guy who offered sponsorship at your last event. Besides battling for your life, you are stuck fighting for control for what is right for the community and what the sponsor wants. I mean, man - after all that you just take the last drops of self respect that you have and think to yourself: why not just take all this energy where I can breathe easier and feel the weight of the world shift from my shoulders. And this is what I am doing. I can never document what happens behind the doors or name any specific events, people or organisation for one simple reason: I still believe in what communities can be. I just choose to not continue because regardless of my good intentions or vision, I am still part of the problem.

..... so what happens next

I walk out the door. Building my next idea. For fun or for business. The baton gets passed. And I stay away a bit so that I do not muddle the waters or meddle with the ones running the game. No backseat driving. I focus on my Young AI Leaders Gweru. I think about bringing PyCon Zimbabwe (think about it, it's not certain) and I build. For the sake of my career. And trust me, I leave grateful. For all the opportunities presented. All the people met. And all the memories created.
